title: Who pays when something goes wrong
summary: Liability is the law's answer to one question: when harm happens, whose pocket pays for it. Four ideas carry most of the answer for a developer: negligence, agency, limited liability, and the narrow cases where courts ignore the company and reach the person behind it.
body:
Mr Shabazz, every project creates the chance of harm to someone, and the law of liability decides who pays for it. Your job as a developer is to know, before anything goes wrong, which pocket each kind of harm will reach, and to make sure it is not your personal one by accident.

Recall

Q. What makes a letter of intent binding or not binding?

A. The words and the conduct. A letter of intent can bind if it says it does or if the parties behave as though they have a deal; a clear statement that only named clauses bind, and that nothing else binds until a definitive agreement is signed, is the main protection.

Q. What is precedent, and why does it matter in a common law system?

A. Precedent is the rule that courts follow earlier decisions of higher courts on the same point of law. It matters because much of the law of negligence and contract lives in decided cases rather than in statutes.

Q. In a sources and uses table, what must be true of the two columns?

A. They must be equal. Every dollar spent on land, hard, soft and finance costs must be matched by a named source of debt or equity.

Why this matters

A developer sits in the middle of a web of people who can harm and be harmed: workers on site, neighbours, future tenants, buyers, lenders and consultants. A single serious incident can produce a claim larger than the profit on the whole project. Whether that claim stays inside one project company, spreads across your other projects, or lands on your house depends on choices you made months or years earlier: the entity, the contracts, the insurance, and whether you behaved in a way that kept the company's separateness real. You cannot make those choices well in the week of the incident. You make them at the start.

LEX speaks today about the principles. Omar joins later in the week on how the corporate structure holds up, and when it does not. Everything below is a concept to understand, not a conclusion about any jurisdiction; verify the law that applies to your project against the primary source and with counsel before you rely on it.

Negligence: the default rule for harm

In plain English, negligence means carelessness that causes harm to someone you should have been careful about. The professional framing breaks it into four elements, and a claimant usually has to prove all four. First, a duty of care, meaning a legal obligation to take reasonable care not to harm a particular class of people. Second, a breach of that duty, meaning conduct below the standard a reasonable person in that position would meet. Third, causation, meaning the breach actually caused the harm and the harm was not too remote. Fourth, damage, meaning a real loss the law recognises.

Professionals are held to the standard of a reasonably competent member of their profession, not the standard of an ordinary person. An engineer is judged against a reasonable engineer. That is why licensing matters: it defines the standard and it names the person.

A worked example, hypothetical. A developer's project company leaves an excavation unfenced over a weekend. A passer-by falls in and is injured. The company owed a duty to people near the site, it fell below the standard by failing to fence, the fall was caused by the open excavation, and the injury is real damage. All four elements line up. The fence would have cost a few thousand dollars. The claim, defence costs and lost time can be many multiples of that. Negligence law is the reason the cheap control is almost always the right one.

Agency: when someone else's act becomes yours

Agency is the relationship where one person, the agent, acts on behalf of another, the principal. When an agent acts within the authority the principal gave, or appeared to give, the principal is bound. A project manager who signs a purchase order within his authority commits the company. A broker who makes a statement to a buyer while marketing your units may expose you to a claim for that statement.

Two forms of authority matter. Actual authority is what you told the agent he could do. Apparent authority is what you led third parties to believe he could do, for example by giving him a title, a letterhead and a history of signing. The second is the dangerous one, because you can be bound by authority you never intended to give.

Closely related is vicarious liability: liability of one person for the wrongful acts of another because of their relationship, most commonly an employer for an employee acting in the course of employment. The employer may not have done anything wrong itself. The relationship is enough. Independent contractors are generally treated differently from employees, but the line is drawn on facts, such as who controls the work, and some duties cannot be handed off at all.

Say that out loud now.

Limited liability: the wall, and its doors

Limited liability means the owners of a company are not personally responsible for its debts beyond what they invested. If a project company with 1,000,000 of equity incurs a 5,000,000 claim, the shareholders can lose the 1,000,000, but the claimant's recovery is limited, in principle, to the company's assets. That is the wall. It is the reason developers hold each project in its own company.

The wall has doors, and you open most of them yourself. You open one when you sign a personal guarantee. You open another when you personally commit a wrong: a director who personally makes a fraudulent statement, or who personally directs unsafe work, can be liable for his own conduct, and the company structure does not shield him from that. Some statutes impose personal liability on directors for certain unpaid amounts, such as some wages, remittances or taxes; verify the statutes that apply to you against the primary source before you rely on any of them. And in narrow cases, a court may disregard the company altogether. Omar takes that last door on Day 4.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A developer owns three projects in one company. Project B has a construction defect that produces a 4,000,000 claim. Projects A and C are healthy and hold 6,000,000 of equity between them. Because all three sit in one company, the claimant can reach all of it. Had each project sat in its own company, the claim would have been limited to Project B's company, and A and C would have been outside its reach, provided the companies were run as genuinely separate. The difference between those two outcomes is a filing fee, a bank account and a habit of discipline.

How the best do it

Large institutional developers commonly hold each project in a single-purpose entity, with its own bank accounts, its own insurance, its own contracts signed in its own name, and its own board decisions recorded in its own minute book. They separate the entity that employs people from the entities that own land. They keep an authority matrix stating who may sign what, up to which amount. None of this is exotic. A small developer can copy all of it from the first project: one company per project, contracts in that company's exact legal name, no mixing of money, and a written list of who can commit the company to what.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is believing the company structure protects you when your own conduct has already removed the protection: a personal guarantee you forgot, a contract signed in your own name, money moved between companies with no record, or a personal instruction that caused the harm. The control is a liability map for every project: which entity signs each contract, which guarantees exist and their limits, which insurance covers which risk, and who has authority to bind each entity. Professional sign-off required: a corporate and litigation lawyer licensed where the project sits.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking liability is about blame. It is about who pays. A beginner asks whose fault it was. A professional asks, before anything happens, which entity and which policy will answer the claim, and works backward to make that answer the right one.

Callback

In week 20 you learned that a contract binds what its words say and that conditions decide when obligations start. Liability is the other half of that picture. Contract allocates risk between people who agreed to it; negligence allocates risk to people who never agreed to anything, like the passer-by at the excavation. And in week 8, protecting the base meant insurance and reserves at the personal level. This week extends the same idea to the project: build the wall before the storm.

Recap

Negligence needs a duty, a breach, causation and damage. Agency means your agents' authorised acts, and sometimes their apparently authorised acts, are yours. Vicarious liability can make you pay for an employee's wrong. Limited liability is a wall around the company, and you open most of its doors yourself. Map who pays before anything goes wrong.

Next: Ford, with Cole, Failure Forensics on the Hyatt Regency walkway collapse.
checklist: Hold each project in its own company, with its own bank account
Sign every contract in the exact legal name of the right entity
Keep a written authority matrix: who may commit each entity, and up to what amount
List every personal guarantee you have given, with its limit and end date
Confirm which insurance policy answers which risk on each project
Fence, light and secure the site as if a stranger will walk onto it tonight
Ask counsel which statutes can make a director personally liable where you build
head: Field checklist
speak: Liability decides whose pocket pays when harm happens, so map it before anything goes wrong. Negligence is the default rule: a duty of care, a breach of the standard, harm caused by that breach, and real damage. Professionals are judged against a reasonably competent member of their profession. Agency means that when someone acts for you within the authority you gave, or appeared to give, you are bound. Vicarious liability can make an employer pay for an employee's wrong even when the employer did nothing wrong itself. Limited liability is a wall around a company: owners can lose what they invested, but in principle not more. You open most of the doors in that wall yourself, with personal guarantees, contracts in your own name, mixed bank accounts, or personal conduct that causes harm. So hold each project in its own company, run it as genuinely separate, and keep a liability map for every project.
terms: Duty of care — a legal obligation to take reasonable care not to harm a particular class of people
Vicarious liability — liability of one person for another's wrongful act because of their relationship, most often employer and employee
Limited liability — the rule that a company's owners are not personally responsible for its debts beyond what they invested

hostile.q: Your project company has 1,000,000 of equity and a construction risk ten times that. What stops a claimant coming after you personally?
hostile.a: Three things, and I can show each one. The company signs every contract in its own name and is run separately, with its own account and minutes. My personal exposure is limited to the guarantees listed on the liability map, each capped and dated. And the project carries insurance sized to the realistic claim, so the first answer to a claim is a policy, not an argument about the corporate wall. Counsel has reviewed the map.

title: Hyatt Regency 1981: the change nobody owned
summary: In 1981 two suspended walkways in a Kansas City hotel atrium collapsed during a crowded event and 114 people died. The cause was a detail changed during shop drawings that doubled the load on a connection, and the deeper cause was that no one clearly owned the check of that change.
rule: Rule 21: No change to a load path, or to any life-safety element, is built until a named, licensed professional has checked it and accepted responsibility for it in writing.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the Hyatt Regency walkway collapse is the clearest lesson in professional liability the building industry has. A small detail changed between design and fabrication, nobody clearly owned the check of that change, and 114 people died. Responsibility that is shared vaguely is responsibility that nobody holds.

Recall

Q. What are the four elements of negligence?

A. A duty of care, a breach of the standard of care, causation linking the breach to the harm, and real damage.

Q. What does the governing law clause of a contract decide, and what does it not decide?

A. It decides which legal system interprets the contract. It does not, by itself, decide which court hears a dispute; that is the forum clause, and the two should be read together.

Q. Why does a pro forma carry a contingency line?

A. Because estimates at early stages are uncertain and some costs cannot be foreseen. Contingency is money set aside for the unknown, sized to how much is still unknown.

Why this matters

As the owner, you will never design a connection or fabricate a beam. But you will run the process through which changes happen: the contractor proposes a substitution, the fabricator asks a question, a deadline presses, and somebody says yes. That process is where liability is created and where lives are protected or lost. Cole is with me today because the case is as much about records and responsibility as it is about steel. The facts below are the broad facts as widely reported from the official investigation and the professional licensing proceedings; verify the detail against those sources before you rely on any of it.

Step 1: Timeline

Late 1970s: the Hyatt Regency hotel in Kansas City, Missouri, was designed and built with a large atrium crossed by suspended walkways at the second, third and fourth floors. During construction there was a partial collapse of the atrium roof, which was reported to have prompted reviews of parts of the structure. The hotel opened in 1980. On 17 July 1981, during a crowded evening event in the atrium, the fourth-floor walkway and the second-floor walkway beneath it fell. 114 people died and many more were injured. A federal investigation followed, and the licensing authority in Missouri later found the engineers responsible for the structural design guilty of professional misconduct, and their licences were revoked.

Step 2: Key decisions

The original design hung both the fourth-floor and second-floor walkways from the same long, continuous rods running down from the ceiling. During the shop drawing stage, the arrangement was changed to two sets of shorter rods: one set held the fourth-floor walkway from the ceiling, and a second set hung the second-floor walkway from the fourth-floor walkway's beams. The change made fabrication and erection easier. The key decision was not the change itself, which can look reasonable on a drawing. It was approving it without a structural check of what it did to the load.

Step 3: Assumptions

The new arrangement meant the connection at the fourth-floor beams carried its own walkway and the walkway below it, roughly doubling the load at that point. The assumption that a fabrication change was a fabrication matter, rather than a structural one, sat at the centre of the failure. The investigation also reported that even the original detail fell short of the capacity the building code required. So the change took an inadequate connection and made it far worse.

Step 4: Incentives

Fast schedules reward quick approval of shop drawings. Fabricators are rewarded for details that are easier to make. Engineers reviewing hundreds of sheets are paid by the project, not by the sheet. Everyone had a reason to move the paper along, and the reviewing process allowed each party to believe someone else had checked the structural consequence.

Say that out loud now.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The atrium roof collapse during construction was a loud signal that the atrium structure deserved scrutiny. Reports also describe communications about the connection detail in which each side appears to have assumed the other had done the calculation. In any project, the warning signs look the same: a substitution submitted with no calculation, a review stamp that says "reviewed for general conformance" with no one stating what was checked, and a question asked by phone and answered by phone with nothing written down.

Step 6: Point of no return

Once the walkways were installed and in service, the structure carried a hidden deficiency that only a load could reveal. The practical point of no return was the approval of the shop drawing without a calculation. After that, the risk sat inside the building, invisible, until a crowd stood on it.

Step 7: Root cause

Diffused responsibility. The design had an engineer of record, but the change passed through a process in which the duty to check the structural effect was not clearly held by one named person who knew he held it. The licensing proceedings answered that question afterwards: the engineer of record cannot delegate away responsibility for the structural integrity of what he seals.

The liability lesson

Three liability ideas from this week meet here. First, the professional standard of care: the engineers were judged against what a reasonably competent structural engineer would have done, and the board found they fell below it. Second, personal professional liability: the licences were personal. A firm can be sued, but the licence that permits a person to seal drawings belongs to that person, and no corporate structure protected it. Third, the owner's position: an owner who hires licensed professionals and runs a disciplined change process is in a far stronger position than one who pressures for speed and approves changes himself. The civil claims that followed the collapse were resolved through settlements; the detail of who paid what is not needed to learn the lesson.

Cole's records check

Cole's question for any change is simple: could you show a stranger, from the documents alone, who checked it, what they checked, and that they accepted responsibility? A hypothetical example. Your contractor proposes replacing cast-in-place balcony slabs with precast units to save three weeks. The precast supplier's engineer designs the units. Your structural engineer of record must check the connections back to the main structure, because that is where the load path changes. The record you want is a written request, a calculation from the supplier's engineer, a written review from your engineer of record stating that the connections were checked against the governing loads, and a revised drawing issued by the engineer of record. If any of those four is missing, the change is not approved. Professional sign-off required: a licensed structural engineer, as engineer of record, and a delegated engineer for any specialty design.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk on your projects is the change that arrives late, looks minor, and saves time. The control is a change procedure that classifies every change touching a load path, a fire separation, an exit or any life-safety system as a design change, never as a fabrication or site matter, and that requires the named engineer of record's written acceptance before work proceeds.

The beginner's mistake

Believing that a review stamp means a check. Read what the stamp says. Many review stamps say the drawing was reviewed for general conformance with the design concept, which is not a statement that every calculation was verified. Ask who checked what, and get the answer in writing.

Rule 21

Rule 21: No change to a load path, or to any life-safety element, is built until a named, licensed professional has checked it and accepted responsibility for it in writing.

Callback

Five lessons ago, in week 20, you learned that a contract binds what its words say. A shop drawing review clause is one of those words: it decides who must check what, and when. On this project the words and the practice allowed each party to believe the other held the duty. And in week 2 you learned the pre-mortem. Run one on every late change: imagine it has failed, then ask who would be asked to explain it. If nobody's name comes to mind, nobody is responsible yet.

Recap

A continuous-rod design was changed during shop drawings into two sets of rods, doubling the load on a connection that was already weak. No one clearly owned the structural check. The walkways collapsed under a crowd. The licences were personal, and so was the responsibility. Rule 21 is the prevention.

Next: Roman, The Money, on what liability costs and how insurance and guarantees change a deal's numbers.
checklist: Classify every change touching structure, fire, exits or life safety as a design change
Require a calculation with every substitution that affects a load path
Get the engineer of record's written acceptance before a structural change is built
Read what each review stamp actually says it checked
Record phone answers to technical questions in writing the same day
Treat any incident during construction as a signal to review the whole system
Never approve a structural change yourself to save time
head: Field checklist
speak: In 1981, two suspended walkways in the atrium of the Hyatt Regency in Kansas City fell during a crowded event, and 114 people died. The original design hung both walkways from continuous rods. During shop drawings, it was changed so that the lower walkway hung from the upper one, which roughly doubled the load on a connection that the investigation found was already below what the code required. The change was easier to build, and nobody clearly owned the structural check of it. The engineers responsible lost their licences, because a seal is personal and responsibility for it cannot be delegated away. For you as owner, the lesson is process. Every change touching a load path or a life-safety system is a design change, and it is not built until a named, licensed professional has checked it and accepted it in writing. That is Rule 21.
terms: Shop drawing — a detailed drawing prepared by a fabricator or contractor showing how a designed element will be made and installed
Engineer of record — the licensed engineer who seals the design and is responsible for its structural integrity
Load path — the route by which a load travels through a structure to the ground

hostile.q: The contractor says this substitution saves three weeks and the supplier's engineer has designed it. Why are you holding up the job for another review?
hostile.a: Because the substitution changes how load reaches the main structure, and only our engineer of record can confirm that the connections still work. The supplier's engineer designed the part, not our building. I've asked for the review in five working days, and if the calculation holds, the three weeks are still largely available. If it does not hold, the review just saved the project.

title: What liability costs: premiums, guarantees and the price of a wall
summary: Liability is a cost even when no claim arrives. Insurance premiums, the expected cost of uninsured claims, and the guarantees you give lenders all belong in the numbers. This lesson prices them and shows how they move return, value and your personal balance sheet.
body:
Mr Shabazz, liability is a cost line whether or not a claim ever arrives. Price it like one: the premium you pay to transfer it, the expected loss you keep, and the guarantee you give a lender, which is a promise with a value even when it is never called.

Recall

Q. What does vicarious liability mean?

A. Liability of one person for another's wrongful act because of their relationship, most commonly an employer for an employee acting in the course of employment.

Q. What is the difference between common law and civil law systems?

A. Common law systems build much of their law from decided cases and precedent; civil law systems rely mainly on comprehensive written codes, with cases playing a more limited formal role.

Q. What is the difference between hard and soft costs?

A. Hard costs are the physical construction of the building and site. Soft costs are everything else needed to deliver it: design, permits, legal, insurance, marketing and similar items.

Why this matters

Lenders and investors read a pro forma for the risks it leaves out. A model that shows insurance as a token line and ignores what happens if a serious claim exceeds the policy is telling the reader that the developer has not thought about liability. A model that prices it is telling them the opposite. For your own wealth, the stakes are sharper: the claims and guarantees that escape the project company land on your personal balance sheet, which is the one you cannot refinance.

Three costs, priced separately

In plain English, liability costs you money three ways. You pay someone to take part of it, which is the insurance premium. You keep the part they will not take, which shows up as deductibles, exclusions and claims above the limit. And you lend your personal credit to the lender, which is the guarantee.

The professional framing gives each a number. The premium is a known cost and sits in soft costs. The retained part is an expected loss, meaning the probability of a loss multiplied by its size, summed across the risks you keep. It belongs in contingency or a dedicated reserve. The guarantee is a contingent liability: it costs nothing today and could cost a great deal later, so it is priced by asking how likely it is to be called and how much would be paid.

A worked example, hypothetical round numbers. A project has a hard cost of 20,000,000. The project's liability and builder's risk insurance costs 1 percent of hard cost, or 200,000. The policies carry a deductible of 100,000 per claim. You judge that, on a build of this size, two claims at the deductible level are a reasonable planning assumption, so you reserve 200,000 for retained losses. You also judge there is a 2 percent chance of a claim of 6,000,000 against a policy limit of 5,000,000, which leaves 1,000,000 uninsured. The expected value of that tail is 2 percent of 1,000,000, or 20,000. These probabilities are judgements, not data; write down where each came from. Total liability cost to carry: 200,000 premium, plus 200,000 retained, plus 20,000 of expected tail, which is 420,000, or about 2.1 percent of hard cost.

How it moves the return

Continue the example. Suppose the project's total cost is 30,000,000 and its stabilised net operating income (NOI), the income after operating expenses and before debt service, is 2,100,000. Yield on cost is NOI divided by total cost, 2,100,000 divided by 30,000,000, which is 7.0 percent. If the original model carried only 100,000 for insurance and nothing for retained losses, the honest total cost is 320,000 higher, at 30,320,000. Yield on cost falls to about 6.93 percent. That looks small. Now remember that the development spread, the gap between yield on cost and the market cap rate, may be only one to one and a half points. Seven hundredths of a point is a few percent of the whole spread, before anything has gone wrong.

The larger effect is in the tail. The 6,000,000 claim, if it happens, leaves 1,000,000 uninsured, and that comes out of equity. On 9,000,000 of equity, it is an 11 percent loss of the money invested, and on a thin-margin deal it can turn a positive internal rate of return negative. That is why lenders ask about policy limits. Your debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), net operating income divided by debt service, does not change because a claim exists, but a lender knows that an uninsured claim can drain the equity cushion that stands in front of its loan.

Say that out loud now.

Pricing a personal guarantee

A personal guarantee is a promise by you to pay if the company does not. Lenders ask for it because it moves your behaviour: a developer whose house is at stake manages the project differently. Treat it as a cost you are giving away for free unless you price it.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A lender offers a 20,000,000 construction loan with a full personal guarantee, or the same loan with a guarantee capped at 25 percent, or 5,000,000, if you accept a rate 0.25 percentage points higher. On an average drawn balance of 12,000,000 over two years, 0.25 points costs 12,000,000 times 0.0025 times 2, which is 60,000. What did the extra 15,000,000 of exposure cost you to give? Suppose your honest judgement is a 3 percent chance that the loan ends in a shortfall, and that if it does, the average shortfall is 8,000,000. Under the full guarantee, your expected payment is 3 percent of 8,000,000, which is 240,000. Under the capped guarantee, the most you pay is 5,000,000, so your expected payment is 3 percent of 5,000,000, which is 150,000. The cap saves you an expected 90,000 for a cost of 60,000. And that understates it, because the full guarantee's worst case is the end of your personal balance sheet, and expected value does not capture ruin. Ratios like a guarantee percentage are commercial practice, not law; they are whatever you and the lender agree.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for the personal balance sheet. A guarantee does not appear on a personal balance sheet as a debt, so it is easy to forget. Keep a separate schedule of contingent liabilities beneath your net worth: every guarantee, its cap, the entity it supports, its end date and what would trigger it. Then compute a stressed net worth: net worth minus the two largest guarantees that could plausibly be called together. If the stressed figure falls below your liquidity floor, the guarantee is too large, whatever the expected value says. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is pricing only the premium and treating the rest as zero. The control is a liability schedule inside every pro forma: premium, deductibles, a retained-loss reserve, a stated tail assumption, and a separate list of every guarantee with its cap and end date, all reviewed at each funding gate. Professional sign-off required: an insurance broker for the programme, and a lawyer for each guarantee's wording.

The beginner's mistake

Signing the guarantee to win the loan and planning to negotiate it down later. Later never comes, because once the guarantee is signed, the lender has no reason to give it back. The time to price it, cap it and set its end date is before you accept the term sheet.

Callback

In week 15 you learned that the internal rate of return can mislead when it hides risk in a small probability of a large loss. A guarantee is exactly that shape: most of the time it costs nothing, and once in a long while it costs everything. And in week 7, the liquidity floor was the amount you will not go below. A guarantee is a call on that floor that someone else gets to decide.

Recap

Liability costs you three ways: the premium, the losses you retain, and the guarantees you give. Price all three, put them in the model, and keep a schedule of contingent liabilities under your net worth with a stressed figure beneath it. Cap and date every guarantee before you sign.

Next: Omar, The Rules, on limited liability and the narrow cases where courts set it aside, with a look at Canada and Guyana.
checklist: Show insurance premium, deductibles and a retained-loss reserve as separate pro forma lines
Write down the source of every probability you use to price a risk
Compare the largest plausible claim with each policy limit
Price each guarantee as an expected payment before accepting it
Cap every guarantee and give it an end date or burn-off
Keep a schedule of contingent liabilities under your personal net worth
Compute a stressed net worth with the two largest guarantees called
head: Field checklist
speak: Liability is a cost even when nothing goes wrong, and it costs you three ways. You pay a premium to transfer some of it. You keep the rest as deductibles, exclusions and claims above the limit, which you price as expected loss: probability times size. And you give lenders your personal guarantee, a promise that costs nothing today and could cost everything later. On a hypothetical 20,000,000 build, a 200,000 premium, a 200,000 reserve for retained claims and a 20,000 expected tail add about 2 percent of hard cost, which can take a meaningful bite out of a thin development spread. A capped guarantee can be worth paying for: in the example, a quarter-point of extra interest cost 60,000 and saved an expected 90,000, while removing the worst case entirely. Keep a schedule of every guarantee under your net worth and test what is left if the two largest are called together.
terms: Expected loss — the probability of a loss multiplied by its size, summed across the risks you keep
Contingent liability — an obligation that exists only if a future event happens, such as a guarantee being called
Deductible — the part of each insured loss that the insured pays before the policy responds

hostile.q: Your insurance line is 1 percent of hard cost. What happens to my equity if you have a claim bigger than your policy limit?
hostile.a: The excess comes out of equity first, so we sized the limit against the largest realistic claim, not the average, and the model carries a stated tail assumption on top of the premium and a retained-loss reserve. If you think the tail is larger than we have assumed, I'd rather buy more limit now than argue about it after a claim; the broker has priced the next layer.

title: The corporate veil: when courts look through the company
summary: A company is a separate legal person, and courts set that separateness aside only rarely. They do it when the company is used as a sham or a façade to dodge an existing obligation, or when it has no real existence apart from its owner. This lesson covers the rule, the narrow exceptions, and how Canada and Guyana approach it.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the corporate veil is strong, and courts pierce it rarely. But when they do, it is almost always because the owner treated the company as a mask rather than as a separate business. Keep the company real and the veil does its job.

Recall

Q. In the Hyatt Regency collapse, what change turned a weak connection into a fatal one?

A. The switch from continuous rods carrying both walkways to two sets of rods, with the lower walkway hung from the upper one, which roughly doubled the load at the fourth-floor connection.

Q. What is the difference between a statute and a regulation?

A. A statute is law passed by the legislature. A regulation is detailed law made under the authority a statute delegates, usually by the government or an agency, and it cannot go beyond what the statute allows.

Q. What is an estimate class, and why does it matter for contingency?

A. An estimate class describes how mature the design behind an estimate is. Less mature estimates carry wider uncertainty, so they need more contingency.

Why this matters

Almost every risk-management decision in development rests on one assumption: that the project company's debts are the company's, not yours. If that assumption fails, every claim, every unpaid supplier and every lender shortfall can reach your personal assets and your other projects. Understanding exactly when the assumption fails is the difference between a structure that protects you and a structure that only looks like it does. This is concept, not advice; verify the law in each jurisdiction against the primary source and with counsel before you rely on it.

Separate legal personality

In plain English, a company is a person in law. It can own land, sign contracts, borrow, sue and be sued, all in its own name. Its debts are its own. The professional term is separate legal personality, and the foundational authority in the common law world is the English House of Lords decision in Salomon v Salomon and Company, decided in 1897, which held that a properly formed company is a separate person even when one individual owns almost all of it and runs it.

The applied point is that the protection does not depend on having many shareholders or a large business. A one-person company is as separate as a listed one. What it depends on is that the company was properly formed and is used as a company.

Piercing the veil: the narrow exceptions

Piercing the corporate veil means a court disregarding a company's separate personality and treating its acts or debts as those of the people behind it. Common law courts describe the grounds in different words, and they move over time, so treat the following as the shape of the doctrine rather than a test to apply. The recurring themes are these.

  • Sham or façade. The company is interposed to evade an obligation the owner already has. The classic pattern is a person who promises not to compete, then sets up a company to compete instead. The court looks through the company because its only purpose is to dodge the promise.
  • Fraud or improper conduct. The company is used as an instrument of fraud, for example moving assets into it to defeat creditors.
  • Complete domination. Courts sometimes speak of the company as the owner's alter ego, meaning it has no real existence separate from the owner, combined with use of that control to cause harm. Control alone is not enough; every sole owner controls his company.

What is not enough, in the common law tradition, is that the result seems unfair, that the company is thinly capitalised, or that one person owns it. Courts have repeatedly said that the veil is not lifted simply because justice seems to require it. The exception is narrow by design, because commerce depends on the rule.

Say that out loud now.

Where the real danger sits

For a developer, the real danger is rarely a court piercing the veil. It is the other routes to personal liability, which do not need the veil to be pierced at all. A personal guarantee is a contract by you. A tort you commit personally, such as a negligent misstatement you make to a buyer, is your tort. Statutes in many jurisdictions make directors personally liable for specified obligations, which can include certain employee wages, tax remittances or environmental duties; verify which apply where you operate against the primary source. And a contract signed in your own name, or in a company name that does not exist yet, may bind you personally.

A worked example, hypothetical. A developer runs three project companies. He pays all of their bills from one bank account in Project A's name, moves money between them with no loan documents, signs contracts on whichever letterhead is nearest, and holds no board meetings. Project B fails owing a supplier 800,000. The supplier's lawyer argues that the three companies are in substance one business run by one man. Even if a court declines to pierce the veil, the supplier may reach Project A's account, because A paid B's bills and its money was mingled, and the developer faces discovery of every transfer. The structure he paid for is now an argument rather than a wall.

Contrast a second hypothetical developer. Each company has its own account. Transfers between companies are documented as loans or equity, approved by resolution and recorded. Contracts are signed in each company's exact legal name. Minutes record major decisions. When Project B fails, its creditors have Project B's assets, and that is all. The second developer did not do anything clever. She did the boring things consistently.

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

A conceptual comparison only; verify against primary source before relying on any of it. Both countries inherited the English common law tradition, so both start from separate legal personality as the rule and treat piercing as a narrow exception developed by the courts. In Canada, companies are formed under federal or provincial corporate statutes, and Canadian courts have generally said they will disregard the corporate form only where it is completely dominated and used as a shield for fraudulent or improper conduct; the precise formulation varies by court and over time, so check current authority in the relevant province. In Guyana, companies are formed under the country's companies legislation, and its courts draw on English and Commonwealth Caribbean authority. Guyana's final court of appeal is understood to be the Caribbean Court of Justice, whose decisions shape the common law across the countries that accept its appellate jurisdiction; confirm the current position before relying on it. The practical lesson is the same in both: statutory director liabilities, guarantees and personal wrongs are far more likely to reach you than a court lifting the veil, and those statutes differ, so each country needs its own review.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a structure that is separate on paper and merged in practice. The control is a separateness checklist, reviewed quarterly by your accountant: own bank account per entity, documented intercompany transfers, contracts in the right name, minutes of major decisions, and adequate insurance in each entity. Professional sign-off required: a corporate lawyer in each jurisdiction where an entity is formed or operates.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking that forming the company is the protection. Forming it creates the possibility of protection. Running it as a separate business is what makes the protection hold.

Callback

In week 19 you learned that law comes from statutes, regulations and decided cases. The veil is a good example of all three at work: statutes create the company, decided cases since 1897 set the rule and its exceptions, and further statutes cut specific holes in the wall for directors. And on Day 1 this week, LEX said you open most of the doors in the wall yourself. Today you saw the doors one by one.

Recap

A properly formed company is a separate person, however small. Courts pierce the veil only in narrow cases: sham, fraud, or total domination used to cause harm. The far bigger risks are guarantees, personal wrongs and statutory director liability. Keep each company genuinely separate, and the wall holds.

Next: Nadia, The Numbers, working through who loses what when a claim hits three different structures.
checklist: Open a separate bank account for every entity before it spends any money
Document every transfer between entities as a loan or equity, with a resolution
Sign every contract in the entity's exact registered name
Hold and minute board decisions for each entity on major matters
Ask counsel which statutes make directors personally liable in each country
Never form a company to avoid an obligation you already have
Have your accountant review separateness every quarter
head: Field checklist
speak: A company is a separate person in law, even when one person owns and runs it. That has been the rule in the common law world since Salomon in 1897. Courts set it aside, which is called piercing the veil, only in narrow cases: where the company is a sham or a façade used to dodge an obligation the owner already had, where it is an instrument of fraud, or where it has no real existence separate from its owner and that control is used to cause harm. Unfairness alone is not enough. For a developer, the bigger danger is personal liability that never needs the veil pierced: guarantees you sign, wrongs you commit personally, statutes that make directors liable, and contracts in your own name. Canada and Guyana both start from the same common law rule, with their own statutes on top. Keep each company genuinely separate in money, contracts and decisions.
terms: Separate legal personality — the rule that a properly formed company is a legal person distinct from its owners
Piercing the corporate veil — a court disregarding a company's separate personality to reach the people behind it
Alter ego — a description courts use for a company with no real existence separate from the person controlling it

hostile.q: All your project companies have the same director, the same address and the same accountant. Why shouldn't I treat them as one business?
hostile.a: Common control is normal and the law expects it. What matters is whether each company is run as itself: each has its own bank account, its own contracts in its own name, documented transfers approved by resolution, its own insurance and its own minutes. I can show you the separateness file for any of them. If you find a transfer that isn't documented, I want to know, because I'd fix it before you did.

title: One claim, three structures: who loses what
summary: A hypothetical 6,000,000 claim hits a developer's portfolio three ways: all projects in one company, each project in its own company, and separate companies with a personal guarantee. Working the numbers step by step shows exactly what the structure protects and what it cannot.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a structure is only as good as the arithmetic of a bad day. Today we run one hypothetical claim through three structures, line by line, and watch where the money comes from each time.

Recall

Q. What does separate legal personality mean?

A. That a properly formed company is a legal person distinct from its owners, with its own assets and its own debts, however small the company and however few its shareholders.

Q. Name the three common remedies for breach of contract.

A. Damages to put the innocent party where performance would have, specific performance in limited cases, and termination where the breach is serious enough.

Q. What is lease-up, and why can a slow one hurt a project?

A. Lease-up is the period from completion to stabilised occupancy. A slow one hurts because operating and debt costs run at full rate while income is still building.

Why this matters

Structure diagrams are reassuring. Numbers are honest. When you can say, with figures, how much a given claim costs you under the structure you chose and under the alternatives, you can make a real decision about how many companies to form, how much insurance to buy and which guarantees to refuse. Everything here is hypothetical, round and simplified, and it assumes the companies are run as genuinely separate; the legal outcome in any real case depends on the facts and the applicable law, which counsel must confirm.

The facts of the example

A developer has three projects, A, B and C. Each has net assets, meaning assets minus liabilities, as follows: A has 4,000,000, B has 2,000,000 and C has 3,000,000. B suffers a liability claim, a defect that causes injury and damage, and the claim is finally settled at 6,000,000. B's liability insurance has a policy limit of 5,000,000, meaning the most the insurer will pay for the claim, and a deductible of 100,000. The developer personally has net worth outside the projects of 1,500,000.

Step 1: what the insurer pays

The insurer pays the claim minus the deductible, up to the limit. The claim of 6,000,000 minus the deductible of 100,000 is 5,900,000. That exceeds the 5,000,000 limit, so the insurer pays 5,000,000. The amount left for the insured is the claim of 6,000,000 minus the 5,000,000 paid, which is 1,000,000. That 1,000,000 is the retained exposure: the part of the claim the insured has to fund itself, made up here of the 100,000 deductible and the 900,000 above the limit.

Check the tie-out: 5,000,000 from the insurer plus 1,000,000 retained equals 6,000,000. Always write the tie-out down. It catches errors in the order you apply deductibles and limits, which policies do not all handle the same way; read the actual wording.

Structure 1: all three projects in one company

Here A, B and C are divisions of a single company with combined net assets of 4,000,000 plus 2,000,000 plus 3,000,000, which is 9,000,000. The retained exposure of 1,000,000 is a debt of that company. The company pays it from its combined assets. Net assets fall from 9,000,000 to 8,000,000. Every project contributes, because there is only one pot. The developer's personal net worth of 1,500,000 is untouched, provided there is no guarantee and no personal wrong.

That looks fine, until you change the claim. Suppose the settled claim were 16,000,000 instead. Insurer pays 5,000,000, retained exposure is 11,000,000, and the single company has only 9,000,000. It is insolvent. Projects A and C, which did nothing wrong, are lost with B.

Say that out loud now.

Structure 2: each project in its own company

Now A, B and C are three separate companies. The claim is against B only. With the 6,000,000 claim, B's retained exposure is 1,000,000 and B has net assets of 2,000,000. B pays it and is left with 1,000,000. A and C are not involved. Total loss to the portfolio: 1,000,000, the same as Structure 1.

With the 16,000,000 claim, B's retained exposure is 11,000,000 against net assets of 2,000,000. B can pay 2,000,000 and is insolvent, leaving 9,000,000 unpaid. A and C keep their 4,000,000 and 3,000,000, a total of 7,000,000 preserved. Compare: under Structure 1 the developer loses all 9,000,000 of net assets; under Structure 2 he loses 2,000,000, the whole of B, and keeps 7,000,000.

Notice two things. For an ordinary claim the two structures cost the same. The separate companies earn their keep only in the tail, the rare large claim. And the unpaid 9,000,000 does not disappear; it is a loss to the claimant. That is the moral weight of this structure, and it is the reason the insurance limit should be sized to the realistic worst claim. Limited liability is a backstop, not a substitute for insurance.

Structure 3: separate companies plus a personal guarantee

Now suppose the developer has personally guaranteed B's obligations to its lender, up to 3,000,000, and the large claim also causes B to default on its loan with a 2,500,000 shortfall. The guarantee is a separate contract with the lender. It does not cover the injury claimant, but it is triggered by B's collapse. The lender calls it, and the developer owes 2,500,000, within the 3,000,000 cap.

His personal net worth of 1,500,000 is not enough. He must find 1,000,000 more, and the likely source is his shares in A and C. Their combined value of 7,000,000 is now under pressure to fund a guarantee on a project that has already failed. The separate companies protected A and C from the claimant, but the guarantee reached them through their owner.

What if the companies were not really separate

Run Structure 2 once more with one change, from Day 4. Suppose B's bills had been paid from A's bank account for a year, and 1,200,000 had moved from A to B with no loan document and no resolution. B's creditors now have an argument that A's money was, in substance, B's money, or that A owes B the undocumented transfers back. Even without a court piercing the veil, the 7,000,000 preserved in the clean version is now partly in dispute, and the legal costs of defending it start at once. Put a number on that dispute in your own model: if even half of the 1,200,000 is recovered from A, the saving from separate companies shrinks by 600,000, before legal fees. Separateness is not a legal formality. In this example it is worth several million dollars on a bad day.

The summary table

Large claim of 16,000,000Structure 1Structure 2Structure 3
Net assets lost9,000,0002,000,0002,000,000
Projects A and CLostKept, 7,000,000Exposed through the owner
Personal net worth of 1,500,000UntouchedUntouchedCalled in full, 1,000,000 short

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is modelling only the ordinary claim, where every structure looks the same, and concluding that structure does not matter. The control is to run every structure decision against three claims: an ordinary one, one at the policy limit, and one at twice the limit, and to include every guarantee in the run. Professional sign-off required: a corporate lawyer on structure and an insurance broker on limits.

The beginner's mistake

Applying the deductible and the limit in the wrong order, or forgetting the deductible entirely. On some policies the deductible erodes the limit; on others it sits beneath it. A difference of 100,000 per claim, repeated, is real money, and the policy wording decides it, not the broker's summary.

Callback

In week 13 you built a sources and uses table where every use had a named source. This lesson is the same discipline applied to a loss: every dollar of a claim must have a named source, whether insurer, company or owner, and the columns must tie. And on Day 3, Roman priced guarantees as expected payments. Today you saw the shape behind that price: in the tail, the guarantee is the path by which one failed project reaches the healthy ones.

Recap

Insurer pays the claim minus the deductible, up to the limit; the rest is retained. For ordinary claims, structure barely matters. For large claims, separate companies preserve the healthy projects, and a guarantee can undo that protection through the owner. Run three claim sizes, every time.

Next: Priya, The Room, at the table when a lender asks for a full personal guarantee.
checklist: Write down each entity's net assets before modelling any claim
Apply deductible and limit exactly as the policy wording says
Write the tie-out: insurer plus retained equals the claim
Run every structure against an ordinary claim, a claim at the limit and a claim at twice the limit
Include every guarantee in the run, with its cap
Size insurance limits to the realistic worst claim, not the average one
Have a lawyer confirm what each structure does in the governing law
head: Field checklist
speak: Run one claim through three structures and the value of each becomes clear. Take a hypothetical 16,000,000 claim against Project B, with a 5,000,000 policy limit and a 100,000 deductible. The insurer pays 5,000,000 and 11,000,000 is retained. If all three projects sit in one company with 9,000,000 of net assets, the company is insolvent and the two healthy projects are lost with the bad one. If each project is its own company, B loses its 2,000,000 and A and C keep their 7,000,000. But if the developer has also guaranteed B's loan and the lender calls 2,500,000, his 1,500,000 of personal net worth is gone and he is 1,000,000 short, which pressures his shares in A and C. For ordinary claims structure barely matters. In the tail it decides everything, and a guarantee is the back door.
terms: Policy limit — the most an insurer will pay under a policy for a claim or in total
Retained exposure — the part of a loss the insured must fund itself, such as the deductible and any amount above the limit
Net assets — total assets minus total liabilities, the value available to absorb losses

hostile.q: If each project is its own company, the injured party may go unpaid. How do you justify that?
hostile.a: I don't rely on the corporate wall to pay claimants; I rely on insurance. The limit on each project is sized to the realistic worst claim, the model tests a claim at twice the limit, and we buy more cover if that test shows a gap we can afford to close. Separate companies stop one failure from destroying unrelated projects and the people working on them. They are a backstop, not a plan to leave anyone unpaid.

title: When the lender asks for your house
summary: A scene: a construction lender's term sheet asks for a full, unlimited personal guarantee. The lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the lender's question, and how to trade for a capped, time-limited guarantee without losing the loan.
body:
Mr Shabazz, when a lender asks for a full personal guarantee, it is rarely asking for your house. It is asking for proof that you will behave well when the project is in trouble. Give it that proof in a cheaper currency than unlimited recourse.

Recall

Q. With a 5,000,000 limit and a 100,000 deductible, what does the insurer pay on a 6,000,000 claim?

A. 5,000,000. The claim minus the deductible is 5,900,000, which exceeds the limit, so the insurer pays the limit and 1,000,000 is retained.

Q. What is the difference between a condition and a promise in a contract?

A. A promise is something a party undertakes to do, and breaking it is a breach. A condition is an event that must happen before an obligation arises; if it does not happen, the obligation never starts.

Q. What is cash-on-cash return?

A. Annual cash flow after debt service divided by the equity invested, a simple measure of the cash yield in a given year.

Why this matters

The guarantee is the single most common way that a developer's personal wealth becomes tied to a project's fate. It is also negotiated in a room where the developer wants the loan badly and the lender knows it. If you walk in without a prepared position, you will sign whatever is on the term sheet. If you walk in with one, you can usually trade an unlimited guarantee for a narrower set of promises that protect the lender against the things it actually fears. What follows is a hypothetical scene with commercial practice, not law; guarantee terms are whatever the parties agree.

The scene

A hypothetical construction loan of 20,000,000 on a mid-size residential project. The lender's credit officer and its relationship manager sit across from you. Your lawyer is beside you. The term sheet says: "Full, unconditional and continuing personal guarantee of all obligations by the principal." The credit officer opens: "This is our standard. We don't do non-recourse construction for developers at your stage."

The question behind the question

Before you answer, ask yourself what risk the guarantee is really covering. Construction lenders typically worry about four things: that the building will not be finished, that it will cost more than budgeted, that the developer will act badly, for example by diverting funds or walking away, and that the market will not support the loan at completion. A full guarantee covers all four with one blunt instrument. A narrower package can cover the first three directly and leave the fourth, market risk, where it belongs, in the equity and the loan sizing.

So the question behind "this is our standard" is: "How do I know you will not leave me with half a building?" Answer that question, and the standard often becomes negotiable.

The lines to say

  • "I understand the concern. Can you tell me which risks matter most to your credit committee on this loan: completion, cost, conduct or market?"
  • "I can offer a completion guarantee, meaning I personally promise the building gets finished, and a cost-overrun guarantee, meaning I fund overruns above budget and contingency."
  • "I can offer a carve-out guarantee, sometimes called a bad-boy guarantee, under which I am personally liable if I commit fraud, divert funds, file for bankruptcy voluntarily without consent or breach specified covenants."
  • "On the payment guarantee, I propose a cap of 25 percent of the loan, falling to zero when the building reaches stabilisation, meaning occupancy and income at the agreed level."
  • "Would a larger equity contribution or a funded interest reserve change what you need from me personally?"

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

  • "Fine, I'll sign whatever you need." You have just given away the most valuable concession in the room for nothing.
  • "There's no risk, it's a great project." The credit officer hears that you have not stress-tested it.
  • "Other lenders don't ask for this." Unless you have a competing term sheet in writing, it is a bluff, and credit officers can tell.
  • "I'll just put my assets in my spouse's name." Never say it, and never do it as a reaction to a guarantee. Transfers made to defeat creditors can be set aside, and saying it destroys trust in a sentence.

A worked trade, hypothetical

Suppose the lender's real worry is completion. You offer: a completion and cost-overrun guarantee, uncapped but limited to the cost of finishing; a carve-out guarantee for bad acts; and a payment guarantee capped at 5,000,000, burning off to 2,500,000 at substantial completion and to zero at stabilisation, defined as 90 percent occupancy for three consecutive months with debt service coverage of at least 1.25 times. In return you accept a rate 0.25 points higher, an interest reserve funded from equity, and monthly reporting. Ratios like these are commercial practice and vary by lender and market. On Day 3, Roman priced a similar trade: about 60,000 of extra interest to remove 15,000,000 of personal exposure. Have that figure in your head, so you can tell the room calmly what you are willing to pay.

When to stay silent

After you make the offer, stop. Let the credit officer respond. The urge to fill silence with extra reassurance or a softer second offer is strong and expensive. Silence tells the room that the offer is considered. If the answer is "I'll have to take it to committee," that is progress, not refusal. Ask what the committee will need to see, write it down, and agree a date.

Holding your state

You will feel the pull of losing the loan. Before the meeting, write your walk-away line: the guarantee terms above which you will look for another lender or more equity. Knowing it is written down keeps your voice level. Breathe slowly and speak at your normal pace; if you notice yourself speeding up, pause and ask a question instead of making a point.

Time and energy on a rotating shift

Do not schedule a negotiation like this on the morning after a night shift. Judgement, patience and the ability to stay quiet all degrade with sleep loss, and a guarantee is a decision with consequences for years. If the only slot the lender offers falls after nights, ask to move it, or take a call to clarify questions and hold the real negotiation later.

Build your preparation into your rotation instead: write the needs list and walk-away line on a day off, rehearse aloud on a second day, and meet on a day when you have slept normally. The lender will never know why you were calm. You will.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is accepting an unlimited guarantee because the term sheet calls it standard. The control is a written guarantee position prepared before every financing: what you will offer, what you will pay for each reduction, and your walk-away line. Professional sign-off required: a finance lawyer reviewing the guarantee wording, especially definitions of default, stabilisation and burn-off.

The beginner's mistake

Negotiating the cap and forgetting the end date. A capped guarantee with no burn-off runs until the loan is repaid, which may be long after the risk it covered has gone.

Callback

In week 3 you learned how anchoring works: the first number on the table pulls everything toward it. "Full, unconditional and continuing" is an anchor. Your counter should be specific and reasoned, not a percentage off the lender's anchor. And in week 6, the "acknowledge, bridge, answer" pattern for hostile questions is exactly how to receive "this is our standard": acknowledge the concern, bridge to the risks behind it, and answer those directly.

Recap

Find the risk behind the guarantee request. Cover completion, cost and conduct with targeted guarantees, cap the payment guarantee and give it a burn-off, and pay for reductions with things the lender values. Prepare the walk-away line in writing, make the offer, then stay silent.

Next: Kema, Quiz and Recap, the week on liability in six questions.
checklist: Write your guarantee position and walk-away line before the meeting
Ask which risk matters most to the lender's credit committee
Offer completion, cost-overrun and carve-out guarantees before any payment guarantee
Cap every payment guarantee and give it a burn-off with a defined trigger
Know what you are willing to pay for each reduction in exposure
Never schedule the negotiation after a night shift
Have a finance lawyer review every definition in the guarantee
head: Field checklist
speak: When a construction lender asks for a full personal guarantee, the question behind it is usually: how do I know you will not leave me with half a building? Answer that question directly. Ask which risk matters most to the credit committee. Then offer a completion guarantee, a cost-overrun guarantee and a carve-out guarantee for bad acts like fraud or diverting funds, and propose a payment guarantee capped at a share of the loan that burns off at completion and stabilisation. Pay for the reductions with things the lender values, such as more equity, a funded interest reserve or a slightly higher rate. Never say you will sign whatever they need, never claim there is no risk, and never talk about moving assets to avoid creditors. Make your offer, then stay silent. Write your walk-away line beforehand, and never negotiate the morning after a night shift.
terms: Carve-out guarantee — a guarantee that makes the principal personally liable only for specified bad acts, such as fraud or diverting funds
Completion guarantee — a promise by the principal that the project will be finished
Burn-off — a reduction of a guarantee's amount when defined milestones are reached

hostile.q: If you won't stand behind the whole loan, why should we believe you'll stand behind the project?
hostile.a: Because I'm standing behind the three things that are in my control: finishing the building, funding overruns above budget and contingency, and behaving properly, and those guarantees are uncapped in scope. The market risk at completion is what the equity and the loan sizing are for, and I'm putting in more equity to prove it. A capped payment guarantee that burns off at stabilisation keeps my exposure tied to the period of real risk.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Liability: the week in six questions
summary: Six questions on negligence, agency, limited liability, the corporate veil and personal guarantees, a Red Pen drill on a project memo with planted defects, and a two-minute boardroom explanation of the week.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week comes down to one habit: before anything goes wrong, know which pocket each kind of harm will reach, and make sure your personal one is reached only where you chose to put it on the line. Today we test that, mark up a flawed memo, and say the week in two minutes.

Recall

Q. What is the question behind a lender's request for a full personal guarantee?

A. Usually: how do I know you will not leave me with half a building? Completion, cost and conduct guarantees answer it more cheaply than unlimited recourse.

Q. What is the difference between a letter of intent and a definitive agreement?

A. A letter of intent records proposed terms, often with only a few clauses binding, such as confidentiality and exclusivity. The definitive agreement is the full binding contract.

Q. What is stabilised net operating income?

A. The net operating income a property earns once lease-up is complete and occupancy has settled at its long-run level, used to value the asset and size permanent debt.

Why this matters

Liability is the area where a developer's personal wealth is most exposed and least visible. Nothing on a balance sheet shows the guarantee you forgot or the contract you signed in your own name. The only defence is understanding, applied early. Test the understanding now, while the cost of a mistake is a wrong answer on a page.

The six questions

Question 1. What must a claimant usually prove in negligence? Answer: a duty of care owed to them, a breach of the standard of care, causation linking the breach to the harm without the harm being too remote, and real damage. Professionals are judged against a reasonably competent member of their profession.

Question 2. What is apparent authority, and why is it dangerous? Answer: the authority a principal leads third parties to believe an agent has, for example through a title, letterhead and history of signing. It is dangerous because it can bind you to commitments you never intended to authorise. The control is a written authority matrix and telling counterparties who may sign.

Question 3. What did the Hyatt Regency walkway collapse teach about responsibility? Answer: that a change to a load path made during shop drawings doubled the load on an already weak connection, and that diffused responsibility let it through. Rule 21: no change to a load path or life-safety element is built until a named, licensed professional has checked it and accepted responsibility in writing.

Question 4. When will a court pierce the corporate veil? Answer: rarely, and in narrow cases such as a sham or façade used to evade an existing obligation, use of the company as an instrument of fraud, or complete domination used to cause harm. Unfairness, thin capital or sole ownership are not enough on their own.

Question 5. On a 16,000,000 claim with a 5,000,000 limit, why do separate project companies matter? Answer: because 11,000,000 is retained. In one company holding 9,000,000 of net assets, every project is lost. In separate companies, only the project with the claim is lost and the others keep their value, unless a personal guarantee reaches them through the owner.

Question 6. What do you offer instead of an unlimited personal guarantee? Answer: completion, cost-overrun and carve-out guarantees, plus a payment guarantee capped at a share of the loan with a burn-off at defined milestones, paid for with things the lender values, such as more equity or an interest reserve.

Say that out loud now.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical memo and find the defects before you read on.

"Liability memo, Project North. The building contract will be signed by me personally until the new company is registered next month, to keep the contractor on schedule. The project company will use the account of our existing company until its own account opens. Our insurance is 1 percent of hard cost, which is standard, so we are covered. The contractor has proposed a lighter steel connection at the canopy, which the supplier's engineer says is fine; I have approved it to save a week. The lender wants a personal guarantee; I signed it because it is standard and we can renegotiate after completion. Because everything is in a company, I have no personal exposure."

The defects. One: signing the building contract personally before the company exists may make the developer personally liable on it, and the contract should be signed by the company once formed, or the situation handled with counsel's advice on pre-incorporation contracts. Two: using another company's bank account mixes money and weakens the separateness of both companies. Three: insurance as a percentage says nothing about limits; the question is whether the limit covers the realistic worst claim. Four: a structural change was approved by the owner on a supplier's word; Rule 21 requires the engineer of record's written acceptance. Five: the guarantee was signed without a cap or burn-off, and renegotiation after signing rarely happens. Six: the final sentence is false: the personal contract, the guarantee and any personal wrong all create personal exposure regardless of the company.

The week on one page

IdeaWhat decides itThe trap
NegligenceDuty, breach, causation, damageSaving a few thousand on a control
AgencyActual and apparent authorityA title and letterhead that bind you
Limited liabilityA properly formed, separately run companyMixed accounts and wrong signatures
The veilSham, fraud, domination used to harmThinking the veil is the main danger
GuaranteesThe contract you signNo cap, no end date

Read the table aloud once, row by row. Where you hesitate, reread that day's lesson tonight.

Boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes to an investment committee. Set a timer. Then compare with this model answer.

"Our liability plan has four layers. First, prevention: the site is secured, the change procedure treats every structural or life-safety change as a design change requiring the engineer of record's written acceptance, and authority to commit the company is written down. Second, transfer: insurance limits are sized to the realistic worst claim, and we tested a claim at twice the limit. Third, containment: each project is its own company with its own account, contracts and minutes, so a failure on one cannot reach the others. Fourth, my personal exposure: I have given completion, cost-overrun and carve-out guarantees, and a payment guarantee capped at 25 percent that burns off at stabilisation. Every guarantee is on a schedule under my net worth. Counsel has reviewed the structure in each jurisdiction."

Scoring your boardroom answer

Score yourself 1 to 5 on four things. Accuracy: did you say anything you could not defend, such as "we have no exposure"? Structure: did you give the layers in order? Composure: did your pace hold when you reached the guarantees? The hard question: did you name the uninsured tail before anyone asked? Record it on your phone, listen once, and do it again tomorrow without notes.

The biggest risk

Believing you have learned liability because you can define the terms. The test is whether your own current arrangements would survive the Red Pen. The control is to apply this week's checklist to one real entity you control within seven days, with counsel.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the company as the whole answer. It is one layer of four, and the weakest one to rely on alone.

Callback

In week 2 you learned inversion: to succeed, first ask how you would fail. This week is inversion applied to your own wealth: ask how a claim could reach you, then close each route. And in week 20, conditions decided when obligations started. A guarantee's burn-off is a condition too: write it as carefully as any condition precedent.

Recap

Negligence, agency, limited liability, the veil and guarantees. Prevent, transfer, contain, and cap what remains personal. Every change to a load path has a named checker. Every guarantee has a cap and an end date.

Next: Elias, First Principles, on how tax works: residence, source, character and flow-through entities.

head: The six questions
speak: This week, one habit: before anything goes wrong, know which pocket each kind of harm will reach. Negligence needs a duty, a breach, causation and damage, and professionals are judged against their peers. Agency means your agents can bind you, including through apparent authority you never meant to give. Limited liability is a wall around each company, and courts pierce it only in narrow cases like a sham or fraud. The bigger risks are the doors you open yourself: guarantees, contracts in your own name, mixed accounts and personal wrongs. The Hyatt Regency collapse showed that a structural change nobody clearly owned can kill, so every such change needs a named, licensed checker in writing. Separate companies protect healthy projects in the tail, but a guarantee can reach them through you. So prevent, transfer with insurance sized to the worst claim, contain with separate companies, and cap and date every guarantee.
terms: Apparent authority — the authority a principal leads third parties to believe an agent has
Pre-incorporation contract — a contract made on behalf of a company before it legally exists, which can bind the person who signed it
Authority matrix — a written list of who may commit an entity to what, and up to which amount

hostile.q: You say each project is ring-fenced. Show me one way a problem on this project could still reach your other companies.
hostile.a: Three ways, and each is controlled. A guarantee I give could make me sell shares in the others, so every guarantee is capped, dated and on my contingent schedule. Undocumented transfers between companies could let creditors argue the money is shared, so every transfer is documented and approved. And a contract signed in the wrong name could bind the wrong company, so contracts are checked against the authority matrix before signature.
